attempts.label: DANDI:000056
attempts.paper_title: Internally organized mechanisms of the head direction sense
attempts.entry_title: Internally organized mechanisms of the head direction sense (Peyrache et al. 2015)
attempts.summary: Most of the paper's main findings held in this data: head-direction cells keep their rates and pair correlations during sleep, thalamic assemblies predict post-subicular cells better than the reverse, and thalamic cells show fast synchrony. The internal signal ran faster in slow-wave sleep than in waking, but about twelvefold where the paper reports tenfold. The large gain of a covariance-based over a tuning-curve-based linear decoder did not reproduce, on an estimator the paper does not define. The connection counts matched only in part, as the dataset holds fewer cell pairs than the paper analysed. Several minor cell and session counts differ, mainly because the files do not mark which sessions the paper kept.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Peyrache, Lacroix, Petersen and Buzsaki (2015) on dandiset 000056, which holds 42 sessions of anterodorsal thalamus and post-subiculum recordings in 7 mice across waking and sleep. It classifies head-direction cells, compares the two structures, and tests the preservation of rates, pair correlations and the activity packet across brain states, the speed of the internal signal, noise correlations, Bayesian and linear decoding, GLM prediction between the structures, fast synchrony and ADn to PoS connections.

outcomes.statement: HD cell ensembles were recorded in 7 mice over 42 open-field sessions with home-cage sleep, with ADn and PoS recorded simultaneously in 3 mice over 21 sessions.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 1; Methods, Recording sessions and behavioral paradigm
outcomes.quote: in 7 mice foraging for food in an open environment (42 sessions) and in their home cages during sleep ... In 3 mice (21 sessions) ADn and PoS recordings were performed simultaneously.
outcomes.notes: Under reading (a), the dandiset holds 7 mice and 41 sessions with an open-field epoch and spikes (Mouse32-140820 has no epochs), both within tolerance. By the files' unit labels, 24 of these sessions in 4 mice hold units of both structures, against 21 (tolerance 2.1) in 3, because Mouse20 has PoS units in 3 sessions, on electrode groups the lab labelled 'postsub' of a device the files call the post-subicular probe. Under reading (b), 40 sessions, 23 of them with both structures (within tolerance) in 4 mice (not). Only the paper's own list of three mice, a variant not taken from the data, gives 21 and 3. The table's 50 sessions are not matched.
deviations: Mice and sessions are counted from the files, and sessions with both structures from the units' region labels; the paper's list of three mice (Supplementary Table 1) is shown as a variant.

outcomes.statement: Per animal, the ADn HD cells (of recorded cells) are 63 (217) in m12, 52 (245) in m17, 15 (49) in m20, 17 (22) in m24, 23 (27) in m25, 37 (55) in m28 and 35 (105) in m32, and the PoS HD cells are 9 (48) in m24, 53 (135) in m25 and 49 (174) in m28.
outcomes.inferred: Numbers from Supplementary Table 1; no sentence states them.
outcomes.notes: Under reading (hd-b), 5 of the 10 HD counts are within tolerance, and under (hd-a) 3. The session-rule variant also gives 5 under (hd-b) and 4 under (hd-a). Mouse32's count cannot be tested, as neither of its sessions holds head direction; its measured 0 is not a measurement, so 9 counts are testable and the outcome would be the same with Mouse32 left out. Over all sessions the dual mice have more ADn HD cells (26, 62 and 74 under hd-a, against 17, 23 and 37), as Supplementary Table 1 counts their ADn cells from a subset of sessions. Recorded units equal the table in Mouse12, Mouse17 and Mouse32 (217, 245, 105), Mouse20 has 48 against 49, and the PoS counts match (48, 135, 174).
deviations: Every session with head direction is used. Supplementary Table 1 counts the ADn cells of Mouse24, 25 and 28 from 2, 3 and 3 of their sessions, which the files do not mark; a reading of the Methods' session rule from the probe depths is shown as a variant for the counts (Methods, Electrodes, surgery and data acquisition).
Tuning curves smooth the spike and occupancy histograms separately before the ratio, a standard choice so that empty 1 degree bins are defined (Methods, Head direction cells).
Mouse32's sessions have no head direction, so its count is untestable (data missing) and recorded as 0 only to keep one value per expected value.

outcomes.quote: 242 out of 720 recorded cells (41% on average) in the anterior thalamus, and 111 out of 357 (31%) cells in the PoS were classified as HD cells.
outcomes.notes: No combination of readings puts all four counts within tolerance. Over all sessions, reading (hd-a) gives 293 thalamic HD cells of 727 classifiable thalamic cells, and 82 PoS HD cells of 337. Reading (hd-b) gives 312 and 120. The per-session mean fractions are 0.53 and 0.22 (hd-a), and 0.57 and 0.33 (hd-b). The PoS counts (337 classifiable, 365 units), the hd-b PoS HD count (120) and the hd-b per-session PoS fraction (0.33) are within tolerance. The thalamic HD counts exceed 242 because the dual mice add sessions the paper did not count; under the session rule they are 207 and 220 of 593. The 727 classifiable thalamic cells are close to the paper's 720 by coincidence, as Mouse32's 105 cells are missing and the ADn cells of sessions the paper discarded in the dual mice are added.

Supplementary Table 1 counts the ADn cells of Mouse24, 25 and 28 from 2, 3 and 3 of their sessions, which the files do not mark; a reading of the Methods' session rule from the probe depths is shown as a variant for the counts (Methods, Electrodes, surgery and data acquisition).
Tuning curves smooth the spike and occupancy histograms separately before the ratio, a standard choice so that empty 1 degree bins are defined (Methods, Head direction cells).
Thalamic cells are units labelled anterodorsal nucleus; the 126 cells of sessions without head direction cannot be classified.

outcomes.statement: In the thalamus, on shanks where at least one HD cell was detected, 71% of the cells were HD cells on average.
outcomes.quote: In the thalamus, when considering only cell ensembles recorded on silicon probe shanks where at least one HD cell was detected, the average proportion of HD cells was 71%
outcomes.notes: On 63 thalamic shank-sessions with at least one HD cell, the mean HD fraction is 0.733 under (hd-a) and the pooled fraction 0.736, both within 0.639 to 0.781. Under (hd-b) they are 0.799 and 0.784, outside the tolerance.

outcomes.statement: Ensembles of 8.4 plus or minus 5.1 (s.d.) units per session were recorded in the ADn and 5 plus or minus 2.8 in the PoS.
outcomes.quote: Ensembles of HD neurons from ADn (8.4 ± 5.1 s.d. units per session) and PoS (5 ± 2.8 s.d.) were recorded by multi-site silicon probes
outcomes.notes: Under HD reading (hd-b) and reading (a), both means are within tolerance and the s.d. are not. ADn HD cells per session are 8.00 plus or minus 4.42 over 39 sessions (mean tolerance 7.56 to 9.24, s.d. 4.59 to 5.61) and PoS HD cells 5.22 plus or minus 4.11 over 23 sessions (4.5 to 5.5, s.d. 2.52 to 3.08). No other combination of readings puts both means within tolerance. The PoS mean rests on the 3 Mouse20 sessions with PoS units and no PoS HD cell, which the files' labels include; without them it is 6.00 over 20 sessions, outside. Under (hd-a) the means are 7.51 and 3.57 (a), 7.51 and 4.10 (b), 10.04 and 8.20 (c).

Every session with head direction is used. outcomes.statement: Sleep was recorded for 5 plus or minus 1 (s.d.) hours per session, before and/or after the open-field exploration.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 2; Methods, Recording sessions and behavioral paradigm
outcomes.quote: neuronal ensembles were monitored during sleep sessions (5 hours ±1 s.d.), before and/or after active exploration in the open field.
outcomes.notes: Under reading (a), the home-cage epochs before and after the open field total 4.99 h on average, with an s.d. of 0.97 h, over 37 sessions with the paper's scoring. Both values are within tolerance. The scored SWS and REM total 3.20 plus or minus 0.57 h (reading b), outside it.

Supplementary Table 1 counts the ADn cells of Mouse24, 25 and 28 from 2, 3 and 3 of their sessions, which the files do not mark; a reading of the Methods' session rule from the probe depths is shown as a variant for the counts (Methods, Electrodes, surgery and data acquisition).
Tuning curves smooth the spike and occupancy histograms separately before the ratio, a standard choice so that empty 1 degree bins are defined (Methods, Head direction cells).

outcomes.statement: ADn HD cells convey 30% more head-direction information than PoS HD cells, 1.44 against 1.11 bits per spike.
outcomes.quote: conveyed 30% more head-direction information than PoS cells (1.44 bit per spike vs. 1.11 bit per spike; see Methods ; Supplementary Fig. 2c ; p < 10 –6 , Mann-Whitney U-test)

statistics.about: exact value in the reporting checklist

outcomes.notes: Under reading (hd-b) with means, ADn HD cells carry 1.38 and PoS HD cells 1.00 bits per spike, both within tolerance, with Mann-Whitney p = 3.9e-11. Under (hd-a) both medians (1.38, 1.14) and both means (1.44, 1.17) are within tolerance, but p = 4.5e-5 does not reach 1e-6. With (hd-b) medians the PoS value (0.87) is outside.

Supplementary Table 1 counts the ADn cells of Mouse24, 25 and 28 from 2, 3 and 3 of their sessions, which the files do not mark; a reading of the Methods' session rule from the probe depths is shown as a variant for the counts (Methods, Electrodes, surgery and data acquisition).
Information uses head-direction frames (25.6 ms) as the time base, the frame nearest each spike giving the intensity (Methods, Information measures), and 10 segments of equal duration.

outcomes.statement: 12% of ADn HD cells and 32% of PoS HD cells were not unimodal, having a second tuning curve peak of at least 50% of the maximal peak rate.
outcomes.quote: 12% of ADn HD cells and 32% of PoS HD cells were not unimodal: their tuning curve showed at least one other peak that was 50% or more than the maximal peak firing rate.
outcomes.notes: Under HD reading (hd-b) and peak reading (a), 12.2% of ADn and 29.2% of PoS HD cells have a second peak of 50% or more, both within tolerance. Under (hd-a) the ADn fraction (10.9%) is within and the PoS fraction (18.3%) is not. Peak reading (b) gives lower fractions (3.4 to 5.1% ADn, 12.2 to 24.2% PoS).
deviations: Tuning curves smooth the spike and occupancy histograms separately before the ratio, a standard choice so that empty 1 degree bins are defined (Methods, Head direction cells).

outcomes.statement: The firing rates of HD neurons are strongly correlated between waking and SWS and between waking and REM sleep, in the ADn and in the PoS.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 3; Figure 2a (ADn n = 215, PoS n = 62 cells)
outcomes.quote: First, the firing rates of HD neurons remained strongly correlated across brain states ( Fig. 2a ).
outcomes.notes: Under the r of at least 0.5 reading, all four correlations pass with p < 0.05. In ADn the waking rates correlate with SWS rates at r = 0.80 and with REM rates at r = 0.86 (hd-a, 274 cells in sessions with both sleep stages). In PoS the values are 0.65 and 0.66 (69 cells). The PoS values are below 0.7 under every cell reading except waking against SWS with rate-a cells (0.73). The cell counts are 245 to 293 ADn and 38 to 100 PoS, against 215 and 62.
deviations: Pearson's r on linear rates; log rates are printed as a variant.
Mouse25-140131 and Mouse25-140204 have no sleep scoring in the files; their open-field epoch is taken as wake and they enter the waking analyses only.

outcomes.statement: The pairwise correlations between HD neuron pairs, within and across structures, are similar across waking, SWS and REM.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 3; Figure 2b (ADn pairs n = 970, PoS pairs n = 92)
outcomes.quote: Second, the pairwise correlations between HD neuron pairs both within and across structures were robustly similar across states ( Fig. 2b )
outcomes.notes: The waking pair correlations predict the SWS and REM ones in every pair type, reading and shank selection, with r from 0.81 to 0.97 (all p < 0.05), so the 0.7 reading holds. The ADn pair counts (1006 to 1425 HD pairs) are above 970.
deviations: Pair correlations over all bins of each state, 300 ms (wake, REM) and 50 ms (SWS), Figure 3a legend.
Mouse25-140131 and Mouse25-140204 have no sleep scoring in the files; their open-field epoch is taken as wake and they enter the waking analyses only.

outcomes.statement: The angular velocity of the internal HD signal, estimated from the temporal profile of pairwise cross-correlograms, is about tenfold faster during SWS than during waking.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 3; Figure 2e,f; Methods, Estimation of angular velocity
outcomes.quote: The angular velocity of the internal HD signal, either estimated by a Bayesian decoder or from the temporal profile of pairwise cross-correlograms ... was approximately tenfold faster during SWS than during waking ( Fig. 2e,f )
outcomes.notes: The SWS speed exceeds the waking speed in most pairs (Wilcoxon p < 0.001 in every reading), but the median SWS to waking ratio is outside 9 to 11. In ADn-ADn pairs it is 11.65 to 12.31 with all fits and 11.04 to 11.71 without the pairs whose fit sits at an end of the speed grid; 95.7% of ADn-ADn pairs are faster in SWS under hd-a and rate-a. In PoS-PoS pairs it is 5.18 to 6.15. It is above 5 in both, the partial criterion. No fitted speed is exactly 0, but every state has fits at 1.5e-14 deg/s, effectively 0 (71 waking, 49 SWS and 99 REM fits below 1 deg/s); they are among the fits at a grid end, which the 11.04 to 11.71 variant leaves out. Pairs without a finite speed in both states are left out. Fits are loose (median residual 0.55 of the cross-correlogram's variance in waking, 0.52 in SWS, 1.04 in REM), and 387 of 1950 pairs have a speed at a grid end in some state.
deviations: Cross-correlograms from 10 ms bins concatenated across the intervals of a state (a standard choice); the coarse grid is 80 speeds from 5 to 5000 deg/s on a log scale (v-c).
Mouse25-140131 and Mouse25-140204 have no sleep scoring in the files; their open-field epoch is taken as wake and they enter the waking analyses only.

outcomes.statement: The angular speed of the Bayesian decoded HD signal is about tenfold faster in SWS than in waking, and similar in REM and waking.
outcomes.quote: The angular velocity of the internal HD signal, either estimated by a Bayesian decoder or from the temporal profile of pairwise cross-correlograms ... was approximately tenfold faster during SWS than during waking
outcomes.notes: The SWS part fails under every reading and the REM part holds in PoS only. At 10 ms steps with the posterior maximum located below the 1 degree grid (a) and decoded waking speed (w-a), the median decoded speed in ADn is 98.7 deg/s in SWS, 19.3 in waking and 12.2 in REM (SWS ratio 5.11, REM ratio 0.63). At the smoothing window (b) the ratios are 6.00 and 0.57; with the actual waking head speed (w-b) they are 1.22 and 0.15 (a) or 4.33 and 0.41 (b). In PoS (4 ensembles with sleep) the SWS ratios are 0.46 to 2.82 and the REM ratio 0.93 (a, w-a) and 1.00 (b, w-a), inside 0.67 to 1.5. As a variant outside the criterion, mean speeds per ensemble give ADn ratios of 10.26 and 0.88 at the smoothing window with the actual waking speed.
deviations: For reading (a) the decoded angle is the posterior maximum located below the 1 degree grid by a parabola through the log posterior (a standard interpolation), as on the grid itself 10 ms speeds come in multiples of 100 deg/s; the grid values are shown beside it. Steps spanning two intervals of a state are left out.
Mouse25-140131 and Mouse25-140204 have no sleep scoring in the files; their open-field epoch is taken as wake and they enter the waking analyses only.

outcomes.statement: The angular velocity of the internal HD signal estimated from cross-correlograms is similar during REM sleep and waking.
outcomes.quote: Angular velocity of the internal HD signal was similar during waking and REM ( Fig. 2e,f ).
outcomes.notes: Both readings hold in ADn-ADn and PoS-PoS pairs under every HD and rate reading. The median REM to waking speed ratio is 0.96 to 1.20, inside 0.67 to 1.5, and no Wilcoxon test of the log ratio reaches p < 0.05 (p from 0.17 to 0.66). Pairs without a positive, finite speed in waking and REM are left out. No fitted speed is exactly 0, but some fits sit at 1.5e-14 deg/s, effectively 0 (71 waking and 99 REM fits below 1 deg/s); they are kept, and the medians do not rest on them.

outcomes.statement: The zero-lag correlation between HD cell pairs falls with the offset of their preferred directions, positive below 60 degrees, negative above it and near zero at about 60 degrees, within and across structures, in waking, REM and SWS.
outcomes.quote: Pairs of neurons with <60° offset showed positive correlations, pairs with >60° offset showed negative correlations, and pairs with approximately 60° offset were uncorrelated ( Fig. 3a ). The relationship between the 0-lag correlation and the preferred angular direction was preserved across brain states

statistics.about: text, all states and pair types
ADn-ADn and ADn-PoS pairs in all three states, and PoS-PoS pairs in waking (reporting checklist)
PoS-PoS pairs, REM (reporting checklist; its SWS value is printed garbled, "p=1xe-8")

outcomes.notes: Under hd-a and rate-b, the zero-lag correlation falls with the preferred-direction offset in all 9 state and pair-type combinations (p < 1e-6 with the absolute offset and with its cosine). The zero crossing is within 54 to 66 degrees in 7 of 9 combinations with 10 degree bins, and 8 of 9 with 20 degree bins. PoS-PoS in SWS crosses at 54 and 108 degrees. Under hd-a and rate-a the PoS-PoS tests reach only p = 5.5e-6 to 7.2e-5 with the absolute offset and 8.2e-6 to 1.3e-4 with its cosine (36 pairs); under hd-b and rate-a all 9 tests pass. ADn-ADn pairs cross at 54 to 59 degrees in every state.
deviations: Mouse25-140131 and Mouse25-140204 have no sleep scoring in the files; their open-field epoch is taken as wake and they enter the waking analyses only.

outcomes.statement: Pairwise correlations of HD cells closer than 60 degrees are stronger in the ADn than in the PoS in every brain state, independently of firing rate differences.
outcomes.quote: HD signal was more strongly preserved in the ADn than in the PoS as shown by the stronger pairwise correlations in any brain state (p < 10 –5 , Mann-Whitney U-test for all pairs closer than 60° in all brain states, n = 345 ADn-ADn pairs; n = 55 PoS-PoS pairs)

statistics.n: 345 ADn-ADn and 55 PoS-PoS pairs closer than 60 degrees

outcomes.notes: Under hd-a and rate-b, pairs closer than 60 degrees are more correlated in ADn than in PoS in every state. The medians are 0.28 against 0.06 in waking, 0.15 against 0.02 in SWS and 0.23 against 0.06 in REM, with Mann-Whitney p = 1.9e-7, 4.6e-8 and 1.7e-6, each below the text's 1e-5. Under hd-a and rate-a, PoS has only 12 pairs and p is 0.03 to 0.045. The ADn pair counts are 328 to 480; 328 (hd-a, rate-a) and 374 (hd-b, rate-a) are within 345 plus or minus 34.5.

outcomes.statement: The stronger correlations in the ADn than in the PoS do not depend on firing rate; in a two-way ANOVA the region effect is significant and the firing rate group effect is not.
outcomes.quote: The brain areas comparison effect was significant (p < 10–7) but the firing rate group effect was not (p > 0.05, two-way ANOVA).
outcomes.notes: Where the region effect reaches p < 1e-7 (12 of 96 readings, all among pairs closer than 60 degrees), the rate-group effect is significant in every one (p from 4.8e-14 to 0.0013). No reading has region p < 1e-7 together with rate-group p > 0.05. Over all pairs the region effect is not found (smallest p 0.029).
deviations: Pairs above 10 Hz are left out of the two-way ANOVA, as the figure has groups below 5 and 5 to 10 Hz only; type 2 sums of squares. The geometric peak rate uses the peak of the HD reading's own fit, and the mean rate is that of the state tested (in the pooled test, each pair's rate in each state), with waking rates as a variant.

outcomes.statement: The activity packets in the ADn and the PoS are coherent with the packet expected from the Bayesian decoded HD, in waking, REM and SWS.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 4; Figure 3b; Methods, Ensemble coherence
outcomes.quote: The actual activity packets, both in the ADn and the PoS, and across brain states, were highly similar to the predictions given by the signal decoded from a Bayesian estimator ( Fig. 3b ) in waking, REM and SWS
outcomes.notes: At the decoder's windows, the median over ensembles of the coherence exceeds 0.05 in both structures and all three states under every reading of distance, reference vectors and summary. The lowest is 0.082 (ADn, SWS, decoded-HD references, correlation distance, median over bins). Every ensemble passes with the mean summary. Other windows were not run. A negative control, the same packets against the expected packet at decoded angles permuted across time bins, shows which readings can fail. With random references it still scores 0.25 to 0.61 and with actual-HD references and the mean summary 0.11 to 0.24 (medians over ensembles), so those readings cannot fail at 0.05. With decoded-HD references and the median summary it is 0.000 in ADn and 0.000 to 0.122 in PoS, against 0.082 to 0.503 for the actual angles; the outcome rests on that reading.
deviations: Only the decoder's own windows (300 ms wake and REM, 50 ms SWS) are run; the other windows of reading (c-c) are not.

Coherence is computed on 3000 time bins drawn at random per state (seeded), a standard choice; the expected packet is the sum of normalised tuning curves weighted by the rates the tuning curves give at the decoded angle (Methods, Ensemble coherence).

outcomes.statement: During waking, the observed correlations of HD cell pairs exceed those expected from independent rate-coded neurons for pairs with overlapping fields (0 plus or minus 15 degrees), fall below them for pairs at 60 plus or minus 15 degrees, and match them only at larger offsets.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 5; Figure 4a,b; Methods, Cross-correlation under the hypothesis of independent firing rate coding scheme
outcomes.quote: However, correlations expected from independent rate-coded neurons could not fully account for the observed pairwise correlations of HD cells ( Fig. 4a ). ... were observed for neuron pairs with overlapping fields (0±15°), with a marked negative signal correlation at 60±15° offset ( Fig. 4b,c ) and the expected correlations became similar to the observed ones only for pairs with larger angular differences.
outcomes.notes: In every reading (HD, rate, lag and scale), the noise correlation is above 0 for pairs within 15 degrees and below 0 for pairs at 60 plus or minus 15 degrees, in ADn-ADn pairs and in pooled pairs. Every Wilcoxon p is below 1e-11. Under hd-a, rate-a and the -50 to +50 ms normalised reading, the ADn-ADn medians are 0.89 and -0.30, and beyond 90 degrees the mean is -0.02.
deviations: The tuning curve of the whole waking epoch is used for the intensity function (n-c), as the criterion says.
Mouse25-140131 and Mouse25-140204 have no sleep scoring in the files; their open-field epoch is taken as wake and they enter the waking analyses only.

outcomes.statement: The correlation excess at 0 degrees and deficit at 60 degrees are stronger for ADn pairs than for PoS pairs.
outcomes.quote: These signal correlations were stronger for ADn than PoS neurons (p < 10 –9 , Kruskal-Wallis one-way analysis of variance; ADn-ADn pairs

statistics.n: ADn-ADn 96 and 200, ADn-PoS 77 and 157, PoS-PoS 29 and 57 pairs, at 0 and 60 degrees

outcomes.notes: Under hd-a and rate-b, with every lag and scale reading, the Kruskal-Wallis test across the three pair types gives p < 0.001 at 0 and at 60 degrees, with ADn-ADn pairs the most extreme. The raw 50 ms reading gives p = 8.5e-9 and 2.3e-13. At 0 degrees there are 101 ADn-ADn, 49 ADn-PoS and 19 PoS-PoS pairs, against 96, 77 and 29. At 60 degrees there are 217, 107 and 31, against 200, 157 and 57.

outcomes.statement: Optimal linear estimates of HD are better when based on spike train covariances than on tuning curve covariances, and the covariance-based estimate almost reaches the performance of a Bayesian decoder.
outcomes.quote: Optimal linear estimates (OLE, see Methods ) of the head-direction were enhanced when using spike train covariances (i.e., including noise correlation) instead of the tuning curve covariances (i.e., signal correlation only). Estimate of HD based solely on the actual covariance of the spike trains almost reached the performance of a non-linear Bayesian decoder
outcomes.notes: Partially reproduced under (hd-b), as proposed after round 2 and agreed in round 3; not reproduced under (hd-a). With the adopted signal OLE (observed variances on the diagonal of Q) and the 25 ADn and 5 PoS hd-a ensembles, the covariance OLE barely beats the signal OLE (median minimum error 12.98 against 13.22 degrees in ADn, 14 of 25, Wilcoxon p = 0.16; PoS 20.96 against 20.96, p = 0.13), so the first part fails. With the 27 ADn and 11 PoS hd-b ensembles it holds in both structures (13.06 against 13.81 degrees, 17 of 27, p = 0.019; 27.79 against 28.37, 9 of 11, p = 0.042). The covariance OLE errors are 1.26 (ADn) and 1.42 (PoS) times the Bayesian decoder's under hd-a and 1.24 and 1.76 under hd-b, so the second part fails in PoS under both. With the variant signal Q (tuning curves throughout), whose signal decoder errs by up to 103 degrees, beyond the 90 degrees of chance, the first part holds in ADn under both readings (p = 6.0e-8 and 1.5e-8) and in PoS under hd-b (p = 0.001) but not under hd-a (p = 0.0625, the floor for 5 pairs). Under (hd-b) the first part holds in both structures with either signal Q. The outcome rests on the estimator assumed here, as the paper defines none, and on the HD reading; whether the claims file's signal Q reads the paper rightly is asked in questions/peyrache-2015.yaml.
deviations: Assumed, as the paper does not define the OLE, weights D = Q^-1 L (Salinas and Abbott 1994), L the correlation of smoothed counts with (cos, sin) of head direction; Q from the counts (covariance OLE) or, for the signal OLE, from the tuning curves read at the head direction off the diagonal with the observed variances on it (independent neurons, the usual signal-only OLE, for the paper's "tuning curve covariances (i.e., signal correlation only)"). Q from the tuning curves throughout, adopted in round 1, is shown as a variant. Windows 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 300, 500 and 1000 ms.
Ensembles are formed from HD cells under (hd-a) and, as asked in round 2, under (hd-b), waking decoding only for the latter; sessions with at least 6 HD cells in a structure.

outcomes.statement: In the ADn the covariance-based OLE is about 50% better than the signal-based OLE, and the gain is significantly larger than in the PoS.
outcomes.quote: In the ADn, where noise correlations were highest for overlapping HD cells, the covariance-based OLE was approximately 50% better than the signal-based OLE ( Fig. 4d,e ), and significantly stronger than in the PoS ( Fig. 4e ; p < 0.05; Mann-Whitney’s U-test; n = 20 ADn and 8 PoS cell ensembles, respectively)

statistics.n: 20 ADn and 8 PoS sessions with 6 or more HD cells

outcomes.notes: With the adopted signal OLE (observed variances on the diagonal), the median ratio of covariance to signal OLE error is 0.99 in ADn (range 0.91 to 1.04) and 0.98 in PoS under hd-a, and 0.99 and 0.99 under hd-b, outside both 0.45 to 0.55 and 0.60 to 0.73, and ADn and PoS do not differ (Mann-Whitney p = 0.28 and 0.82). With the variant signal Q (tuning curves throughout) the ADn ratio is 0.25 under both HD readings, also outside, as that signal decoder works poorly, and ADn against PoS gives p = 0.17 and 0.067. No reading gives either part. There are 25 ADn and 5 PoS ensembles under hd-a and 27 and 11 under hd-b, against 20 and 8. The outcome rests on the estimator assumed here.
deviations: Assumed estimator and ensembles, as for fig4d-ole-near-bayesian.

outcomes.statement: The HD signal decoded with a Bayesian decoder from HD cells faithfully tracks the head direction of the waking mouse.
outcomes.source: Methods, Bayesian reconstruction of Head-Direction; Figure 1c
outcomes.quote: These estimates faithfully tracked the head position in the waking mouse.
outcomes.notes: The median over ensembles of the median absolute decoding error is 10.2 degrees in 25 ADn ensembles (maximum 13.1) and 14.4 degrees in 5 PoS ensembles (maximum 25.1) with whole-epoch tuning curves. Cross-validated, it is 10.7 and 14.8. All are under 30 degrees, against 76 to 77 degrees with the head direction shifted by 10 s. With hd-b ensembles (27 ADn, 11 PoS), decoded as the round-2 verifier asked, it is 10.1 and 15.0 degrees (10.7 and 16.1 cross-validated).
deviations: Mouse25-140131 and Mouse25-140204 have no sleep scoring in the files; their open-field epoch is taken as wake and they enter the waking analyses only.

outcomes.statement: Tuning curves of HD cells computed during sleep from the HD signal decoded from the other structure are remarkably similar to their waking tuning curves.
outcomes.quote: tuning curves were remarkably similar during sleep to that of waking ( Fig. 5a,b ;
outcomes.notes: The tuning curves against decoded HD correlate with the waking tuning curves with medians of 0.92 (REM), 0.90 (SWS) and 0.98 (waking) for 51 to 64 PoS HD cells decoded from ADn, and 0.87, 0.81 and 0.93 for 43 to 52 ADn HD cells decoded from PoS. Both bin readings give the same medians within 0.01. Every median is above 0.5.
deviations: Target cells are HD cells under reading (hd-a); decoding uses the hd-a HD cells of the other structure.
Mouse25-140131 and Mouse25-140204 have no sleep scoring in the files; their open-field epoch is taken as wake and they enter the waking analyses only.

outcomes.statement: The HD signal decoded from ADn assemblies gives tuning curves of PoS HD cells more similar to their waking tuning curves than the signal decoded from PoS assemblies does for ADn HD cells, in all brain states.
outcomes.quote: However, the HD signal extracted from ADn assemblies resulted in tuning curves more similar to actual HD fields than the HD signal decoded from PoS assemblies, in all brain states
outcomes.notes: PoS cells decoded from ADn have higher correlations than ADn cells decoded from PoS in every state. Under reading (a), Mann-Whitney p = 7.0e-7 in waking, 5.0e-4 in SWS and 0.039 in REM; reading (b) gives 1.5e-7, 4.7e-4 and 0.042. The counts are 64 and 52 cells in waking, against 86 and 92.

outcomes.statement: ADn assemblies predict PoS spike trains reliably in all brain states.
outcomes.quote: ADn assemblies predicted PoS spike trains reliably in all brain states ( Fig. 5d,e ; p < 10 –10 in all brain states, Wilcoxon’s signed rank test, n = 86)
outcomes.notes: ADn HD cell assemblies predict PoS HD cells above chance in every state. Of the PoS targets (HD cells under either reading) kept as positively predicted at one window or more, 122 (waking), 99 (SWS) and 101 (REM) have median best-window information of 0.67, 0.63 and 0.49 bits per spike, Wilcoxon p = 9.2e-22, 5.7e-18 and 2.7e-18, each below 1e-10. With hd-a targets, 81, 66 and 69 are kept (the waking count within 86 plus or minus 8.6), p = 5.4e-15, 1.6e-12 and 5.2e-13. The selection makes the test one-sided by construction; without it p is 5.0e-22, 2.5e-18 and 1.1e-18. The count with either-reading targets (122) is above the tolerance. Assemblies and targets are HD cells (readings g-b, g-c); the all-cell readings were not run.
deviations: Run in glm_peyrache_2015.ipynb on the 20 sessions with HD cells in both structures (Mouse20 has none in PoS), with HD cells as assembly and targets (readings g-b and g-c; hd-a or hd-b, and hd-a targets as a variant), 7 readout windows from 10 to 1000 ms on a log scale (reading g-d), and at most the first 20 minutes of each state, for time.

The GLM is fitted by Newton's method with a line search; the log likelihood is concave in the weights (the link is convex and log-concave), so its maximum is the one the Methods' derivative-free search finds. Each fold is iterated to convergence from the fit to all segments.

outcomes.statement: The optimal readout windows of the ADn to PoS prediction are similar in waking and REM, median 123 ms and 133 ms, and shorter in SWS, median 79 ms.
outcomes.quote: Optimal readout windows were similar between waking and REM (median: 123 ms and 133 ms respectively) and shorter during SWS (median: 79 ms).
outcomes.notes: Recorded as blocked (too_large) in the first two rounds, on a GLM timing the notebook did not print; the round-2 verifier found the block unsupported, and the claim was then run with the dense window grid in glm_windows_peyrache_2015.ipynb, which prints its own run time. Partially reproduced, as proposed after round 2 and agreed in round 3. The grid has 26 readout windows (23 at 20 per decade from 20 to 251 ms s.d.) for PoS targets of ADn assemblies. For the 122, 101 and 99 kept PoS targets (HD under either reading), the median best window is 168 ms in waking, 178 ms in REM and 63 ms in SWS read as the s.d. (a), and 396, 419 and 149 ms as the full width (b), against 123, 133 and 79 ms; none is within tolerance, and the SWS median is below both others in every variant (SWS against waking and REM, Mann-Whitney p = 1.6e-18 and 6.9e-12; waking against REM p = 0.96). With hd-a targets (a) they are 200, 224 and 67 ms. The best window is at an end of the grid for 10 waking, 22 REM and 6 SWS targets, so the REM median is loose.
deviations: Run in glm_windows_peyrache_2015.ipynb as for fig5d-adn-predicts-pos-reliably (HD cells as assembly and targets, at most the first 20 minutes of each state, Newton's method), for PoS targets of ADn assemblies only, with readout window s.d. of 10 ms, 20 to 251 ms at 20 per decade, 500 ms and 1000 ms.

outcomes.statement: PoS assemblies predict ADn spike trains more weakly than ADn assemblies predict PoS spike trains, in all brain states and especially during SWS.
outcomes.quote: In the reverse direction, PoS cell assemblies predicted spike trains of ADn neurons more weakly, especially during SWS
outcomes.notes: With the kept targets of fig5d-adn-predicts-pos-reliably, PoS targets are better predicted from ADn assemblies than ADn targets from PoS assemblies in every state, medians 0.67 against 0.55 bits per spike in waking (Mann-Whitney p = 0.0095), 0.63 against 0.17 in SWS (6.3e-11) and 0.49 against 0.33 in REM (0.020). The gap is largest in SWS (0.72 of the PoS median, against 0.19 and 0.32). With hd-a targets p = 2.6e-4, 4.2e-9 and 0.014, the gap again largest in SWS. Without the selection, REM gives p = 0.059. The ADn target count (176 in waking, 162 with hd-a targets) is far above 62, as the ADn HD cells of every session of the dual mice are targets here.

outcomes.statement: Cross-correlograms between ADn HD cell pairs show fast oscillatory synchrony in windows of about 1 to 5 ms, at 130 to 160 Hz, in all brain states.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 7; Figure 6a,c; Supplementary Figure 7a; Discussion, paragraph 4
outcomes.quote: Spectral analysis of cross-correlation functions between pairs of HD cells in the ADn revealed strong oscillatory spiking dynamics activity in windows of approximately 1–5 ms
outcomes.notes: For ADn HD pairs on different shanks (492 per state), the mean power of the z-scored cross-correlograms above 80 Hz peaks at 165 Hz in waking, 175 Hz in SWS and 165 Hz in REM, all within 117 to 176 Hz. With same-shank pairs included, the peak moves to the top of the frequency grid (285 to 300 Hz).
deviations: The jitter null is the expectation of the jittered cross-correlogram (the cross-correlogram convolved with a 20 ms box) with its Poisson s.d., in place of 100 jittered trains; assumed, for time. Power is averaged over lags within +-25 ms; frequencies 50 to 300 Hz in 5 Hz steps.
Mouse25-140131 and Mouse25-140204 have no sleep scoring in the files; their open-field epoch is taken as wake and they enter the waking analyses only.

outcomes.statement: Fast synchrony between ADn HD cell pairs decreases with the difference of their preferred directions, in all brain states.
outcomes.quote: The degree of synchrony decreased with the magnitude of difference between the preferred head directions of the neurons ( Fig. 6b ; p < 10 –10 ; Kruskal-Wallis test, n = 970 ADn HD cell pairs) in all brain states
outcomes.notes: With the peak z within 5 ms and the ADn HD pairs on different shanks (492 per state, 1476 pooled, the measured value; 1320 waking pairs with same-shank pairs included), the three states pooled give Kruskal-Wallis p = 2.2e-24 across 30 degree offset groups. The mean falls from 11.6 (0 to 30 degrees) to 3.0 (150 to 180 degrees). In each state p < 0.05 with the same fall (waking p = 1.4e-5, SWS 5.1e-14, REM 2.2e-6). Waking alone does not reach 1e-10. The fall from the first to the last group is what the criterion asks for; it is not monotonic, as in every state the mean rises again in the 120 to 150 degree group (2.94 to 3.65 pooled). The zero-lag z of all pairs is negative (same-shank pairs).
deviations: The same jitter null as fig6a-fast-oscillation.

outcomes.statement: Putative monosynaptic connections were found in 4.45% of 6960 ADn to PoS pairs and in 0.35% from PoS to ADn; among ADn and PoS pyramidal cell pairs (3394), feed-forward ADn to PoS connections were twice as likely as PoS to ADn (0.41% against 0.18%).
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 7; Figure 7a,b; Supplementary Figure 7b; Methods, Detection of mono-synaptic connections
outcomes.quote: cross-correlation analyses between pairs of ADn-PoS neurons revealed putative synaptic connections in a fraction of the pairs (4.45% of 6960 pairs from ADn to PoS, 0.35% from PoS to ADn ... When only ADn and PoS pyramidal cell pairs were considered (3394 pairs), we found putative synaptic connections in both directions ( Supplementary Fig. 7b ) but the probability of feed-forward connections from the ADn to the PoS was twice as high as the PoS to ADn feedback direction (0.41% ADn-PoS pairs versus 0.18% PoS-ADn pairs; p = 0.014, binomial test)

statistics.about: ADn to PoS against PoS to ADn, pyramidal pairs
statistics.n: 3394 ADn HD cell and PoS pyramidal cell pairs, 14 and 6 connected (reporting checklist)

outcomes.notes: The ADn to PoS fraction is within tolerance; the pair count, the PoS to ADn fraction and the pyramidal fractions are not. Over all 4765 ADn by PoS pairs of the sessions with both structures, 4.11% are connected ADn to PoS (Methods' baseline; 4.01% with the jitter baseline) and 0.44% PoS to ADn, against 0.35% (0.315 to 0.385). 4765 is every ADn by PoS pair the dandiset holds (the sum over sessions of ADn units times PoS units), so 6960 cannot be reached. The paper's three mice give 4699 pairs (4.17% and 0.45%), and without Mouse28-140314, which has no head direction, 4111 (4.57% and 0.51%). Among the 1583 pairs of ADn HD and PoS pyramidal cells, 1.07% are connected ADn to PoS and 0.44% PoS to ADn (17 and 7 pairs), against 0.41% and 0.18% over 3394. The direction holds against the PoS to ADn proportion (binomial p = 0.0009) and not against one half (17 of 24, p = 0.064).

PoS pyramidal cells from the dataset's mean waveforms (buzcode_mean_waveform), with a Morlet power spectrum after 4x cubic upsampling, a standard choice.

outcomes.statement: ADn HD cell spikes are associated with high-frequency oscillations of the PoS LFP.
outcomes.quote: ADn cell spiking was associated with high frequency LFP oscillations in the PoS ( Fig. 7c )
outcomes.notes: Within 5 ms of ADn HD cell spikes, the 80 to 250 Hz PoS LFP has more power than at jittered spike times (median ratio 2.85, 126 of 175 cells, Wilcoxon p = 2.5e-12) and than at random times (3.17, p = 1.4e-13), in the sessions with both structures. verifications.reviewed: Round 1, the handover of the first author run (executed notebook without conclusions or summary, hd.py, the claims file), transcripts/peyrache-2015/verifier-1-report.md.

disagreements.reason: Cell 11 gives 7 mice and 41 sessions with an open field (reading a). The 21 sessions and 3 mice with both structures come from the paper's mouse list (DUAL), not from the data. By the unit labels it is 24 sessions in 4 mice (Mouse20 has PoS units), which is outside tolerance. The archive also describes Mouse20 as anterior thalamus and the post-subiculum.

Cell 28, reading (b), the SWS/wake ratio is 6.0 (decoded wake) or 4.3 (actual), REM/wake 0.57 or 0.41. Reading (a) is degenerate (problem 3), as bayes_decode returns whole degrees, so speeds over 10 ms steps come in multiples of 100 deg/s; a mean, or decoding finer than 1 degree, would have been needed.

verifications.reviewed: Round 2, the full executed notebooks of the first revision (reproduce_peyrache_2015.ipynb, glm_peyrache_2015.ipynb), hd.py, the claims file and this record, transcripts/peyrache-2015/verifier-2-report.md.

disagreements.reason: I disagree with the block (too_large). It rests on the GLM run taking "21.1 minutes", with the longest session at 952 s. G cell 2 prints "analysed 26 sessions in 12.2 min", and G cell 4 gives 561 s as the longest session. At the record's own factor of 3.3, the denser grid would take about 40 minutes, under the 60-minute limit. It should be run with the denser window grid, or the block justified with timing the notebook actually prints.

verifications.reviewed: Round 3, the two changes of outcome proposed after round 2 (fig4d-ole-near-bayesian and fig5e-readout-windows), with the re-executed reproduce_peyrache_2015.ipynb and glm_windows_peyrache_2015.ipynb, transcripts/peyrache-2015/verifier-3-report.md.

paper_notes.statement: The Results cite the Methods for the optimal linear estimator of Fig. 4d,e, but the Methods have no OLE section. Question for the authors: how were the signal (tuning curve) and covariance OLEs built (which Q and L, which windows, whether cross-validated)? With the standard estimator and the observed variances on the diagonal of the signal Q, the two OLEs barely differ (median error ratio 0.99 in ADn); with Q from the tuning curves throughout, the covariance OLE error is a quarter of the signal OLE error (0.25), as that signal decoder errs near chance in some ensembles.

Question for the authors: which sessions of Mouse24, 25 and 28 gave the ADn cells of Supplementary Table 1, and how was the rule of discarding sessions separated by less than three days without a probe move applied? The depth-based reading keeps 3, 6 and 3 sessions, against 2, 3 and 3, and drops one Mouse17 session the table counts.

Question for the authors: how was the angular speed of the decoded HD computed (Fig. 2e)? With the decoder of the Methods (posterior maximum on 1 degree bins, 10 ms bins) the median speed at 10 ms steps is 0 or 100 deg/s; located below the grid it gives an ADn SWS to waking ratio of 5.1, and at the smoothing window 6, not 10. Mean speeds per ensemble give 5.3 to 14.8.

Neither the paper nor the dandiset links analysis code. The dandiset's only related resource is the paper, and the paper says only that the analyses were run in Matlab, so the von Mises fit, the Rayleigh test, the cross-correlogram estimate of angular velocity and the coherence measure cannot be checked against the authors' code.

entries.name: peyrache-2015
entries.title: Internally organized mechanisms of the head direction sense (Peyrache et al. 2015)
entries.description: Tests the findings of Peyrache, Lacroix, Petersen and Buzsaki (2015) on dandiset 000056, which holds 42 sessions of anterodorsal thalamus and post-subiculum recordings in 7 mice across waking and sleep. It classifies head-direction cells, compares the two structures, and tests the preservation of rates, pair correlations and the activity packet across brain states, the speed of the internal signal, noise correlations, Bayesian and linear decoding, GLM prediction between the structures, fast synchrony and ADn to PoS connections.
